claim: The human brain contains over 100 billion neurons and glial cells.
source: For example, the human brain contains over 100 billion neurons and glial cells (Herculano-Houzel, 2009), all of which are precisely connected to form a functioning organ.
evidence: Supported by citation to Herculano-Houzel, 2009

claim: Alan Turing's reaction-diffusion mechanism consists of an activator molecule that can make more of itself, an inhibitor molecule that inhibits production of the activator, and a mechanism for diffusing these two molecules.
source: For example, Alan Turing's reaction-diffusion mechanism, which consists of an activator molecule that can make more of itself, an inhibitor molecule that inhibits production of the activator, and a mechanism for diffusing these two molecules (Turing, 1952), has been suggested to create the diverse array of biological patterns found in fish stripes (Kondo and Asal, 1995), in seashells (Meinhardt, 1995), and in fur and skin coloration such as those of giraffes and lizards (Manukyan et al., 2017; Walter et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turing, 1952

claim: Turing's reaction-diffusion mechanism has been suggested to create biological patterns found in fish stripes.
source: For example, Alan Turing's reaction-diffusion mechanism, which consists of an activator molecule that can make more of itself, an inhibitor molecule that inhibits production of the activator, and a mechanism for diffusing these two molecules (Turing, 1952), has been suggested to create the diverse array of biological patterns found in fish stripes (Kondo and Asal, 1995), in seashells (Meinhardt, 1995), and in fur and skin coloration such as those of giraffes and lizards (Manukyan et al., 2017; Walter et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kondo and Asal, 1995

claim: Turing's reaction-diffusion mechanism has been suggested to create biological patterns found in seashells.
source: For example, Alan Turing's reaction-diffusion mechanism, which consists of an activator molecule that can make more of itself, an inhibitor molecule that inhibits production of the activator, and a mechanism for diffusing these two molecules (Turing, 1952), has been suggested to create the diverse array of biological patterns found in fish stripes (Kondo and Asal, 1995), in seashells (Meinhardt, 1995), and in fur and skin coloration such as those of giraffes and lizards (Manukyan et al., 2017; Walter et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Meinhardt, 1995

claim: Turing's reaction-diffusion mechanism has been suggested to create biological patterns in fur and skin coloration such as those of giraffes and lizards.
source: For example, Alan Turing's reaction-diffusion mechanism, which consists of an activator molecule that can make more of itself, an inhibitor molecule that inhibits production of the activator, and a mechanism for diffusing these two molecules (Turing, 1952), has been suggested to create the diverse array of biological patterns found in fish stripes (Kondo and Asal, 1995), in seashells (Meinhardt, 1995), and in fur and skin coloration such as those of giraffes and lizards (Manukyan et al., 2017; Walter et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manukyan et al., 2017 and Walter et al., 1998

claim: Dissociated different germ layers of embryonic amphibian cells re-aggregate and sort out into layers according to their cell type.
source: This concept was first demonstrated in 1955 by Townes and Holtfreter, who dissociated different germ layers of embryonic amphibian cells, mixed them together, and found that these cells re-aggregated and sorted out into layers according to their cell type (Townes and Holtfreter, 1955).
evidence: Supported by citation to Townes and Holtfreter, 1955

claim: Differential adhesion has been shown to organize nerve bundles in the Drosophila visual system.
source: Differential adhesion has also been shown to organize nerve bundles in the Drosophila visual system (Schwabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwabe et al., 2014

claim: Altering cell number in the C. elegans nervous system gives rise to an emergent, well-ordered pattern of dendrite arbors.
source: For example, we recently showed how altering cell number in the C. elegans nervous system gives rise to an emergent, well-ordered pattern of dendrite arbors (Yip and Heiman, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yip and Heiman, 2016

claim: The amphid contains 12 sensory neurons and two glial cells.
source: The amphid contains 12 sensory neurons and two glial cells.
evidence: Direct statement about amphid structure

claim: Each amphid neuron extends a single unbranched dendrite that terminates at the nose tip in a sensory cilium that senses environmental stimuli.
source: Each neuron extends a single unbranched dendrite that terminates at the nose tip in a sensory cilium that senses environmental stimuli (Ward et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ward et al., 1975

claim: Amphid dendrites fasciculate to form one of four bilaterally symmetric nerve bundles that constitute the sensory structures of the head.
source: Together, these dendrites and their associated glial processes fasciculate to form one of four bilaterally symmetric nerve bundles that constitute the sensory structures of the head.
evidence: Direct statement about amphid bundle structure

claim: Amphid dendrites appeared to be ordered consistently within the bundle relative to one another based on analysis of four animals.
source: Based on analysis of four animals, Ward and colleagues noted that amphid dendrites appeared to be ordered consistently within the bundle relative to one another, commenting that 'Although individual worms are not precise replicas of each other down to the finest details, they are remarkably exact copies' (Ward et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ward et al., 1975

claim: Recent EM studies are consistent with amphid dendrites being ordered consistently within the bundle.
source: These observations are also consistent with recent EM (Doroquez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Doroquez et al., 2014

claim: Amphid dendrites do not grow outwards to the nose from a stationary cell body, but instead form by anchoring to the embryonic nose tip while the cell bodies migrate away together.
source: Amphid dendrites do not grow outwards to the nose from a stationary cell body, but instead form by anchoring to the embryonic nose tip while the cell bodies migrate away together, a phenomenon known as retrograde extension (Heiman and Shaham, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heiman and Shaham, 2009

claim: Amphid dendrite fasciculation can be studied independently of outgrowth and guidance.
source: Thus, amphid dendrite fasciculation can be studied independently of outgrowth and guidance.
evidence: Logical inference from the retrograde extension mechanism

claim: Promoters with single-cell-specificity are readily available for all amphid neurons.
source: Finally, promoters with single-cell-specificity are readily available for all amphid neurons, allowing us to easily visualize and genetically manipulate any single amphid neuron in live animals.
evidence: Statement about available genetic tools

claim: Dendrites in newly hatched larvae were too close together to be reliably resolved using traditional widefield deconvolution microscopy.
source: Using traditional widefield deconvolution microscopy, we found that dendrites in newly hatched larvae were too close together to be reliably resolved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Dendrites in older larvae and adults were readily discerned despite each dendrite being only about 0.5 μm in diameter.
source: but dendrites in older larvae and adults were readily discerned despite each dendrite being only about 0.5 μm in diameter, close to our effective resolution limit (Figure 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Doroquez et al., 2014; Ward et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation, reference to figures, and citations to Doroquez et al., 2014 and Ward et al., 1975

claim: Amphid dendrites are tightly fasciculated throughout larval growth.
source: We found that dendrites are tightly fasciculated throughout larval growth (Figure 2A) (average longest pairwise distance ± standard deviation: 24 hr, 0.88 ± 0.09 μm; 48 hr, 1.11 ± 0.22 μm; 72 hr, 1.51 ± 0.25 μm).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements and reference to Figure 2A

claim: The average longest pairwise distance between amphid dendrites at 24 hr is 0.88 ± 0.09 μm.
source: We found that dendrites are tightly fasciculated throughout larval growth (Figure 2A) (average longest pairwise distance ± standard deviation: 24 hr, 0.88 ± 0.09 μm; 48 hr, 1.11 ± 0.22 μm; 72 hr, 1.51 ± 0.25 μm).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experimental data

claim: The average longest pairwise distance between amphid dendrites at 48 hr is 1.11 ± 0.22 μm.
source: We found that dendrites are tightly fasciculated throughout larval growth (Figure 2A) (average longest pairwise distance ± standard deviation: 24 hr, 0.88 ± 0.09 μm; 48 hr, 1.11 ± 0.22 μm; 72 hr, 1.51 ± 0.25 μm).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experimental data

claim: The average longest pairwise distance between amphid dendrites at 72 hr is 1.51 ± 0.25 μm.
source: We found that dendrites are tightly fasciculated throughout larval growth (Figure 2A) (average longest pairwise distance ± standard deviation: 24 hr, 0.88 ± 0.09 μm; 48 hr, 1.11 ± 0.22 μm; 72 hr, 1.51 ± 0.25 μm).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from experimental data

claim: The approximate doubling in bundle width may reflect an increased diameter of each dendrite and thus the entire bundle.
source: The approximate doubling in bundle width may reflect an increased diameter of each dendrite and thus the entire bundle, and roughly corresponds to the overall doubling in length of the head during these stages.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed data

claim: Amphid dendrites are well-ordered, especially in younger animals.
source: We found that amphid dendrites are well-ordered, especially in younger animals (Figure 2B,C; left plots).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 2B,C

claim: Amphid dendrite order exhibits a switch point, which itself is stereotyped.
source: Interestingly, although dendrite order is stereotyped, it is not uniform along the length of the bundle. Instead, it exhibits a switch point, which itself is stereotyped (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 2B,C

claim: Close to the nose tip, AFD is predominantly in the middle of the amphid bundle.
source: Close to the nose tip, AFD (blue) is predominantly in the middle, but following the switch point, ASE (red) takes over as the middle dendrite for the rest of the length of the bundle.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: Following the switch point, ASE takes over as the middle dendrite for the rest of the length of the amphid bundle.
source: Close to the nose tip, AFD (blue) is predominantly in the middle, but following the switch point, ASE (red) takes over as the middle dendrite for the rest of the length of the bundle.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: AWA is rarely in the middle of the amphid bundle, and only for short segments.
source: AWA (yellow) is rarely in the middle, and only for short segments (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 2B,C

claim: Amphid dendrite order is maintained throughout larval development, although it becomes increasingly 'noisy' with age.
source: This order is maintained throughout larval development, although it becomes increasingly 'noisy' with age.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: A different set of three amphid dendrites (AWA, AWC, ASG) are also well-ordered and exhibit a similar switch point.
source: We further confirmed these results by showing that a different set of three amphid dendrites (AWA, YFP; AWC, CFP; ASG, mCherry) are also well-ordered and exhibit a similar switch point (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: The position of the switch point correlates with the position where the socket glial cell process joins the bundle.
source: We measured the average positions of the AUA dendrite ending and the amphid socket glial cell, and found the position of the switch point does not correlate with the AUA ending, but does correlate with the position where the socket glial cell process joins the bundle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: The position of the switch point does not correlate with the AUA dendrite ending.
source: We measured the average positions of the AUA dendrite ending and the amphid socket glial cell, and found the position of the switch point does not correlate with the AUA ending, but does correlate with the position where the socket glial cell process joins the bundle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: Lack of cilia had no effect on fasciculation or dendrite order.
source: We found that lack of cilia had no effect on fasciculation or dendrite order (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation in daf-19; daf-12 mutants and reference to figures

claim: Dendrite order does not depend on normal patterns of neuronal activity.
source: As cilia are required for normal neuronal activity, this result also implies that dendrite order does not depend on normal patterns of activity.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation that cilia-less mutants have normal dendrite order

claim: In mec-8 mutants, amphid dendrite endings are disorganized and diverge into separate, isolated channels in the sheath glial cell.
source: Whereas wild-type dendrite endings enter the amphid sheath glial cell in a stereotyped order and converge into a central channel, in mec-8 mutants the amphid dendrite endings are disorganized and diverge into separate, isolated channels in the sheath glial cell (Figure 3C) (Perkins et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perkins et al., 1986 and reference to Figure 3C

claim: Despite disorganized dendrite endings in mec-8 mutants, overall dendrite fasciculation and order along the length of the amphid bundle remain normal.
source: Despite this disorganization, we found that overall dendrite fasciculation and order along the length of the amphid bundle remain normal (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to figures

claim: Proper arrangement of amphid cilia is not required for dendrite order.
source: Altogether, our results show that proper arrangement of amphid cilia is not required for dendrite order.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations in daf-19; daf-12 and mec-8 mutants

claim: Amphid dendrites form cell junctions with the sheath glial cell.
source: Amphid dendrites form cell junctions with the sheath glial cell, and the sheath glial cell secretes factors that promote the normal development and function of the dendrite sensory endings (Bacaj et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bacaj et al., 2008

claim: The sheath glial cell secretes factors that promote the normal development and function of the dendrite sensory endings.
source: Amphid dendrites form cell junctions with the sheath glial cell, and the sheath glial cell secretes factors that promote the normal development and function of the dendrite sensory endings (Bacaj et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bacaj et al., 2008

claim: In glia-ablated animals, dendrites remain well-ordered and mostly unchanged from wild type.
source: In glia-ablated animals, we found dendrites to remain well-ordered (blue color bar) and mostly unchanged from wild type (red color bar), suggesting that sheath glia are not required to maintain dendrite order after the amphid bundle initially develops (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to figures

claim: Sheath glia are not required to maintain dendrite order after the amphid bundle initially develops.
source: In glia-ablated animals, we found dendrites to remain well-ordered (blue color bar) and mostly unchanged from wild type (red color bar), suggesting that sheath glia are not required to maintain dendrite order after the amphid bundle initially develops (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inference from experimental observation in glia-ablated animals

claim: The conspicuous cell biological features of amphid dendrites – their cilia and cell-cell junctions – are not required for dendrite fasciculation or order.
source: Together, our data suggest that the conspicuous cell biological features of amphid dendrites – their cilia and cell-cell junctions – are not required for dendrite fasciculation or order.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations in multiple mutants

claim: SAX-7/L1CAM and the large extracellular matrix molecule DIG-1 are required for dendrite and axon fasciculation.
source: Previous studies in C. elegans and other organisms have shown that cell adhesion molecules such as SAX-7/L1CAM and the large extracellular matrix molecule DIG-1 are required for dendrite and axon fasciculation (Burket et al., 2006; Bénard et al., 2006; Sasakura et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burket et al., 2006; Bénard et al., 2006; Sasakura et al., 2005

claim: Few studies in any system have explored how CAMs affect the ordering of axons or dendrites within a bundle.
source: However, few studies in any system have explored how CAMs affect the ordering of axons or dendrites within a bundle (Lin et al., 1994; Schwabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 1994 and Schwabe et al., 2014

claim: dig-1 mutants exhibited readily apparent defasciculation defects in 24% of animals.
source: As a positive control, we found that dig-1 mutants exhibited readily apparent defasciculation defects in this assay (24% of animals, Table 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from dye-filling screen

claim: ptp-3(mu256) mutants exhibit amphid defasciculation defects in 14% of animals.
source: Using this approach, we identified seven additional CAM mutants that cause defasciculation defects (ptp-3, sax-7, vab-1, sax-3, cdh-4, unc-40 and nrx-1; Table 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from dye-filling screen shown in Table 1

claim: sax-7(ky146) mutants exhibit amphid defasciculation defects in 12% of animals.
source: Using this approach, we identified seven additional CAM mutants that cause defasciculation defects (ptp-3, sax-7, vab-1, sax-3, cdh-4, unc-40 and nrx-1; Table 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from dye-filling screen shown in Table 1

claim: cdh-4(rh310) mutants exhibit amphid defasciculation defects in 6% of animals.
source: Using this approach, we identified seven additional CAM mutants that cause defasciculation defects (ptp-3, sax-7, vab-1, sax-3, cdh-4, unc-40 and nrx-1; Table 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from dye-filling screen shown in Table 1

claim: A redundant system of CAMs contributes to dendrite fasciculation.
source: Interestingly, even the most pronounced defects among these are weakly penetrant (<25%) suggesting that a redundant system of CAMs contributes to dendrite fasciculation.
evidence: Inference from the observation that defasciculation defects are weakly penetrant

claim: Loss of sax-7 was previously observed to cause 'loosening' of amphid dendrites in some animals.
source: Loss of sax-7 was previously observed to cause 'loosening' of amphid dendrites in some animals, along with other defects, but this aspect of its phenotype has not been pursued (Sasakura et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sasakura et al., 2005

claim: cdh-4 encodes a Fat-like cadherin characterized by the large number of cadherin repeats in its extracellular domain.
source: cdh-4 encodes a Fat-like cadherin characterized by the large number of cadherin repeats in its extracellular domain (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement about protein structure with reference to Figure 4A

claim: In C. elegans, cdh-4 has been implicated in axon fasciculation in the dorsal and ventral nerve cords.
source: In C. elegans, cdh-4 has been implicated in axon fasciculation in the dorsal and ventral nerve cords (Schmitz et al., 2007; Schmitz et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmitz et al., 2007 and Schmitz et al., 2008

claim: The rh310 allele of cdh-4 introduces a premature stop codon in the extracellular domain.
source: We used the rh310 allele, which introduces a premature stop codon in the extracellular domain (Figure 4A)(Schmitz et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmitz et al., 2008 and reference to Figure 4A

claim: In cdh-4 mutants, dendrite order was lost despite the bundle remaining intact and well-fasciculated.
source: In the remaining 16/21 animals, we found that dendrite order was lost despite the bundle remaining intact and well-fasciculated (Figure 4B), with the ASE, AFD, and AWA dendrites occupying the middle position with approximately equal frequency along the entire length of the bundle (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to figures

claim: In cdh-4 mutants, ASE, AFD, and AWA dendrites occupy the middle position with approximately equal frequency along the entire length of the bundle.
source: In the remaining 16/21 animals, we found that dendrite order was lost despite the bundle remaining intact and well-fasciculated (Figure 4B), with the ASE, AFD, and AWA dendrites occupying the middle position with approximately equal frequency along the entire length of the bundle (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 4D

claim: Dendrite order in cdh-4 mutants is not significantly different from random.
source: Permutation tests confirmed that dendrite order in this population is not significantly different from random (light shading in blue color bar) and is significantly different from wild type (dark shading in red color bar).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using permutation tests

claim: Dendrite order in cdh-4 mutants is significantly different from wild type.
source: Permutation tests confirmed that dendrite order in this population is not significantly different from random (light shading in blue color bar) and is significantly different from wild type (dark shading in red color bar).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis using permutation tests

claim: Dendrite order defects are present in cdh-4 mutants at 24 hr (L2/L3 stage).
source: We found that dendrite order defects are also present in younger animals (24 hr, L2/L3 stage; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Cell body positioning appeared normal in cdh-4 mutants in newly hatched larvae.
source: However, cell body positioning appeared normal in newly hatched larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: CDH-4 plays an essential role in specifying dendrite order despite having a more redundant role in overall fasciculation.
source: Our results show that, although cdh-4 mutants exhibit only partially penetrant defects in fasciculation, they show nearly complete loss of dendrite order within the bundle, suggesting CDH-4 plays an essential role in specifying dendrite order despite having a more redundant role in overall fasciculation.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations in cdh-4 mutants

claim: ptp-3 encodes a receptor-like protein tyrosine phosphatase that is part of the leukocyte antigen related (LAR) family of proteins.
source: ptp-3 encodes a receptor-like protein tyrosine phosphatase that is part of the leukocyte antigen related (LAR) family of proteins that play important roles in nervous system development, including axon guidance and fasciculation (Ackley et al., 2005; Clandinin et al., 2001; Dunah et al., 2005; Harrington et al., 2002; Krueger et al., 1996; Maurel-Zaffran et al., 2001; Wills et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: LAR family proteins play important roles in nervous system development, including axon guidance and fasciculation.
source: ptp-3 encodes a receptor-like protein tyrosine phosphatase that is part of the leukocyte antigen related (LAR) family of proteins that play important roles in nervous system development, including axon guidance and fasciculation (Ackley et al., 2005; Clandinin et al., 2001; Dunah et al., 2005; Harrington et al., 2002; Krueger et al., 1996; Maurel-Zaffran et al., 2001; Wills et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: sax-7 encodes a homolog of the L1 cell adhesion molecule that is widely involved in neurodevelopment, including axon guidance and fasciculation.
source: sax-7 encodes a homolog of the L1 cell adhesion molecule that is also widely involved in neurodevelopment, including axon guidance and fasciculation, and is disrupted in a human neurological disorder called L1 syndrome (Bénard et al., 2012; Chen and Zhou, 2010; Kim and Emmons, 2017; Sakurai, 2012; Sasakura et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: L1 cell adhesion molecule is disrupted in a human neurological disorder called L1 syndrome.
source: sax-7 encodes a homolog of the L1 cell adhesion molecule that is also widely involved in neurodevelopment, including axon guidance and fasciculation, and is disrupted in a human neurological disorder called L1 syndrome (Bénard et al., 2012; Chen and Zhou, 2010; Kim and Emmons, 2017; Sakurai, 2012; Sasakura et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: ptp-3(mu256) and sax-7(ky146) exhibit amphid defasciculation defects with low penetrance.
source: As expected from our dye-filling assays, ptp-3(mu256) and sax-7(ky146) exhibit amphid defasciculation defects with low penetrance (pink traces in Figure 5C,F and representative images in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to figures

claim: Fasciculation defects in ptp-3(mu256) and sax-7(ky146) become progressively more severe throughout larval development.
source: In both ptp-3(mu256) and sax-7(ky146), fasciculation defects become progressively more severe throughout larval development (Figure 5C,F), consistent with previous observations that SAX-7 is required for the maintenance of nervous system architecture (Bénard et al., 2012; Sasakura et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation, reference to figures, and citations

claim: SAX-7 is required for the maintenance of nervous system architecture.
source: In both ptp-3(mu256) and sax-7(ky146), fasciculation defects become progressively more severe throughout larval development (Figure 5C,F), consistent with previous observations that SAX-7 is required for the maintenance of nervous system architecture (Bénard et al., 2012; Sasakura et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bénard et al., 2012 and Sasakura et al., 2005

claim: In older animals (72 hr, adult stage), ptp-3(mu256) and sax-7 exhibited random dendrite order, similar to cdh-4.
source: In older animals (72 hr, adult stage), ptp-3(mu256) and sax-7 exhibited random dendrite order, similar to what we observed in cdh-4 (Figure 5D,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to figures

claim: Dendrite order defects in ptp-3 and sax-7 are specific to the PTP-3B isoform and to SAX-7.
source: These defects are specific to the PTP-3B isoform and to SAX-7, as dendrite order is not affected by loss of PTP-3A alone (ptp-3(ok244), Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) or by disruption of adhesion molecules that interact genetically or physically with SAX-7 or its homologs in other contexts (DMA-1, CLR-1, IGCM-1) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) (Dong et al., 2013; Islam et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2016; Salzberg et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in multiple mutants and citations

claim: Cell bodies remained ordered normally relative to each other in newly hatched animals for both ptp-3 and sax-7.
source: While sax-7 has been reported to exhibit cell body positioning defects in ~10% of newly hatched animals (Sasakura et al., 2005), we found that cell bodies remained ordered normally relative to each other in newly hatched animals for both ptp-3 and sax-7 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to figures

claim: In ptp-3(mu256) animals at the 24 hr (L2/L3) and 48 hr (L4) time points, the bundle is arranged in a stereotyped order that resembles wild type but has the switch point shifted towards the nose.
source: In ptp-3(mu256) animals at the 24 hr (L2/L3) and 48 hr (L4) time points, the bundle is arranged in a stereotyped order that resembles wild type but has the switch point shifted towards the nose, such that ASE (red) occupies the middle position throughout nearly the entire bundle (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 5D

claim: In sax-7 animals at the 24 hr (L2/L3) time point, the middle position is occupied with roughly equal frequency by ASE and AWC but almost never by AFD.
source: In sax-7 animals at the 24 hr (L2/L3) time point, the middle position is occupied with roughly equal frequency by ASE (red) and AWC (yellow) but almost never by AFD (blue), indicating that dendrite order is not random.
evidence: Supported by experimental observation

claim: As sax-7 animals reach the 48 hr (L4) time point, the order of dendrites appears increasingly random.
source: As animals reach the 48 hr (L4) time point, the order of dendrites appears increasingly random, and by 72 hr (adult) it is indistinguishable from the random order seen in cdh-4 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 5G

claim: Loss of PTP-3 and SAX-7 together leads to even greater defasciculation and increased randomness of dendrite order at the 48 hr (L4) time point.
source: Loss of PTP-3 and SAX-7 together (ptp-3(mu256); sax-7(ky146) double mutant) leads to even greater defasciculation and increased randomness of dendrite order at the 48 hr (L4) time point (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H,I).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to figures

claim: PTP-3 and SAX-7 are required to establish the wild-type dendrite order during early development.
source: Together, our results suggest that PTP-3 and SAX-7 are required, first, to establish the wild-type dendrite order during early development and, second, to maintain dendrite order throughout larval growth.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations in ptp-3 and sax-7 mutants

claim: PTP-3 and SAX-7 are required to maintain dendrite order throughout larval growth.
source: Together, our results suggest that PTP-3 and SAX-7 are required, first, to establish the wild-type dendrite order during early development and, second, to maintain dendrite order throughout larval growth.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations in ptp-3 and sax-7 mutants

claim: Loss of a single CAM can generate a dendrite order that is neither wild type nor random.
source: The observation that loss of a single CAM can generate an order that is neither wild type nor random suggests that dendrites might normally 'choose' from among several potential neighbors, and that these preferences are altered when a given CAM is removed.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations in ptp-3 and sax-7 mutants

claim: Cell-specific differences in the expression level of a single CAM helps to determine neighbor preferences among Drosophila retinal axons.
source: Recent work has shown that cell-specific differences in the expression level of a single CAM helps to determine neighbor preferences among Drosophila retinal axons (Schwabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwabe et al., 2014

claim: ptp-3bpro is expressed at low but detectable levels in many cells, including several amphid neurons, with highest expression in AWB and ASE.
source: We found that ptp-3bpro is expressed at low but detectable levels in many cells, including several amphid neurons, with highest expression in AWB and ASE (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 5E

claim: sax-7Spro is expressed throughout the nervous system and, within the amphid, is consistently expressed in AWC, ASE, and ASK.
source: We found that sax-7Spro is expressed throughout the nervous system and, within the amphid, is consistently expressed in AWC, ASE, and ASK (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 5H

claim: The differential expression of ptp-3 and sax-7 is consistent with a model in which these and other CAMs determine dendrite neighbor preferences through differential adhesion, differences in signaling, or both.
source: The differential expression we observe using these synthetic reporter constructs is consistent with a model in which these and other CAMs determine dendrite neighbor preferences through differential adhesion, differences in signaling, or both.
evidence: Inference from expression pattern observations

claim: Loss of either sax-7 or ptp-3 causes amphid dendrites to initially take on a non-random arrangement that is distinct from wild type.
source: To summarize, we found that loss of either sax-7 or ptp-3 causes amphid dendrites to initially take on a non-random arrangement that is distinct from wild type.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations

claim: In both sax-7 and ptp-3 mutants, dendrite order becomes increasingly random over time, and correlates with increased defasciculation.
source: In both sax-7 and ptp-3 mutants, this order becomes increasingly random over time, and correlates with increased defasciculation.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations

claim: sax-7 and ptp-3 are required for ordering dendrites within the amphid bundle.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that sax-7 and ptp-3 are required for ordering dendrites within the amphid bundle, such that loss of either CAM causes a weakly-penetrant defasciculation phenotype and a highly-penetrant change in dendrite order.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations

claim: Loss of either sax-7 or ptp-3 causes a weakly-penetrant defasciculation phenotype and a highly-penetrant change in dendrite order.
source: Taken together, our data suggest that sax-7 and ptp-3 are required for ordering dendrites within the amphid bundle, such that loss of either CAM causes a weakly-penetrant defasciculation phenotype and a highly-penetrant change in dendrite order.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations

claim: Misexpression of SAX-7 in more cells and at higher levels led to subtle yet reproducible changes in the wild-type order, shifting the switch point more posteriorly.
source: Misexpression of SAX-7 did not change the dendrite order drastically, but misexpression in more cells and at higher levels led to subtle yet reproducible changes in the wild-type order, shifting the switch point more posteriorly (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental observation and reference to Figure 6D

claim: SAX-7 may play an instructive role in specifying the arrangement of amphid dendrites, possibly by contributing to patterns of differential adhesion.
source: These results do not exclude that additional CAM-independent mechanisms might contribute to dendrite order, but suggest that SAX-7 may play an instructive role in specifying the arrangement of amphid dendrites, possibly by contributing to patterns of differential adhesion.
evidence: Inference from SAX-7 misexpression experiments

claim: Amphid dendrites are ordered within the bundle, and this order is maintained over time.
source: In this study, we took advantage of the simple nervous system of C. elegans to quantitatively assess the arrangement of individual dendrites within a nerve bundle. We found that amphid dendrites are ordered within the bundle, and this order is maintained over time.
evidence: Summary of main findings

claim: Dendrite order does not depend on the conspicuous cell biological structures at the dendrite endings (sensory cilia and dendrite-glia junctions).
source: Dendrite order does not seem to depend on the conspicuous cell biological structures at the dendrite endings (sensory cilia and dendrite-glia junctions) but is instead imposed by multiple CAMs expressed by the neurons.
evidence: Summary of findings from experiments with daf-19, mec-8, and glia ablation

claim: Dendrite order is imposed by multiple CAMs expressed by the neurons.
source: Dendrite order does not seem to depend on the conspicuous cell biological structures at the dendrite endings (sensory cilia and dendrite-glia junctions) but is instead imposed by multiple CAMs expressed by the neurons.
evidence: Summary of findings from CAM mutant experiments

claim: Loss of the Fat-like cadherin CDH-4 leads to randomized arrangement of dendrites.
source: Loss of the Fat-like cadherin CDH-4 leads to randomized arrangement of dendrites, whereas loss of PTP-3/LAR or SAX-7/L1CAM, or misexpression of SAX-7, can cause dendrites to take on an altered non-random order.
evidence: Summary of findings from cdh-4 mutant experiments

claim: Loss of PTP-3/LAR or SAX-7/L1CAM can cause dendrites to take on an altered non-random order.
source: Loss of the Fat-like cadherin CDH-4 leads to randomized arrangement of dendrites, whereas loss of PTP-3/LAR or SAX-7/L1CAM, or misexpression of SAX-7, can cause dendrites to take on an altered non-random order.
evidence: Summary of findings from ptp-3 and sax-7 mutant experiments

claim: Misexpression of SAX-7 can cause dendrites to take on an altered non-random order.
source: Loss of the Fat-like cadherin CDH-4 leads to randomized arrangement of dendrites, whereas loss of PTP-3/LAR or SAX-7/L1CAM, or misexpression of SAX-7, can cause dendrites to take on an altered non-random order.
evidence: Summary of findings from SAX-7 misexpression experiments

claim: The arrangement of dendrites within the bundle is determined by multiple CAMs, and altering their relative expression can lead to novel arrangements.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that the arrangement of dendrites within the bundle is determined by multiple CAMs, and altering their relative expression can lead to novel arrangements.
evidence: Inference from all experimental observations

claim: In the mammalian cortex, dendrites arising from neurons in different cortical layers come together to form microcolumns.
source: In the mammalian cortex, dendrites arising from neurons in different cortical layers come together to form microcolumns (Fleischhauer et al., 1972; Fleischhauer, 1974; Peters and Walsh, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fleischhauer et al., 1972; Fleischhauer, 1974; Peters and Walsh, 1972

claim: Axons projecting from the retina and the olfactory bulb exhibit stereotyped arrangements within their respective bundles.
source: Axons projecting from the retina, as well as the olfactory bulb, have provided evidence that neurites can exhibit stereotyped arrangements within their respective bundles, for example reflecting their topographic or dorsal-ventral origins, or the chronological order of their outgrowth (Chan and Chung, 1999; Walsh and Guillery, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chan and Chung, 1999 and Walsh and Guillery, 1984

claim: Stereotyped arrangements of axons arise during development and can affect axon targeting.
source: Recent studies have shown that these arrangements arise during development and can affect axon targeting (Cioni et al., 2018; Imai et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cioni et al., 2018; Imai et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2013

claim: A certain growing (G) axon selectively adheres to a defined partner (P) axon in a specific bundle in grasshoppers.
source: In classical studies using grasshoppers, Goodman and colleagues showed that a certain growing (G) axon selectively adheres to a defined partner (P) axon in a specific bundle.
evidence: Supported by reference to classical studies by Goodman and colleagues

claim: If the P axon is ablated in grasshoppers, the G axon does not adhere to other axons in this bundle or in any neighboring bundles.
source: If the P axon is ablated, the G axon does not adhere to other axons in this bundle or in any neighboring bundles, suggesting a remarkable degree of selective adhesion between G and P (Bastiani et al., 1984; Lin et al., 1994; Raper et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bastiani et al., 1984; Lin et al., 1994; Raper et al., 1984

claim: The organization of Drosophila visual system cartridges reflects differential expression levels of N-cadherin, with higher-expressing L neurites forming an adhesive core surrounded by lower-expressing R axons.
source: In a more recent study, Schwabe et al. studied the cartridges of the Drosophila visual system, which exhibit an invariant organization in which neurites from lamina cells (L) are surrounded by photoreceptor (R) axons. They found that this organization reflects differential expression levels of N-cadherin, with the higher-expressing L neurites forming an adhesive core surrounded by the lower-expressing R axons (Schwabe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwabe et al., 2014

claim: Neurites can exhibit stereotyped neighbor relationships within a bundle.
source: These studies led to two major principles, which are further supported by the work described here: first, that neurites can exhibit stereotyped neighbor relationships within a bundle and, second, that these relationships can arise from differential adhesion.
evidence: Synthesis of findings from multiple studies

claim: Stereotyped neighbor relationships within a bundle can arise from differential adhesion.
source: These studies led to two major principles, which are further supported by the work described here: first, that neurites can exhibit stereotyped neighbor relationships within a bundle and, second, that these relationships can arise from differential adhesion.
evidence: Synthesis of findings from multiple studies

claim: Multiple adhesion molecules can act in concert to specify distinct relationships among many neurites, in a pattern that is more complex than 1:1 pairing or inside:outside relationships.
source: Importantly, our study introduces a third principle – that multiple adhesion molecules can act in concert to specify distinct relationships among many neurites, in a pattern that is more complex than the 1:1 pairing of G and P axons or the inside:outside relationship of L and R neurites.
evidence: Inference from the current study's findings

claim: Bundle order does not reflect the developmental order of neurite outgrowth in C. elegans.
source: One trivial explanation would be that bundle order reflects the developmental order of neurite outgrowth, with the oldest neurite – typically the pioneer axon or dendrite – in the center, and the youngest neurites on the periphery. However, this is not the case in C. elegans, the only organism in which the birth order and neurite position of every neuron is known.
evidence: Statement based on knowledge of C. elegans development

claim: VD motor neurons are born post-embryonically and extend axons along the ventral nerve cord after the nerve cord is established, yet their axons insinuate deeply into the ventral nerve cord to adhere closely to the DD motor neurons.
source: As an example, the VD motor neurons are born post-embryonically and extend axons along the ventral nerve cord after the nerve cord is established, yet their axons insinuate deeply into the ventral nerve cord to adhere closely to the DD motor neurons, a functionally similar set of motoneurons that are born much earlier and lie at the center of the ventral nerve cord (White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 1976 and White et al., 1986

claim: Neurites 'choose' their neighbors within a bundle, possibly with functional consequences.
source: This and similar examples suggest that neurites 'choose' their neighbors within a bundle, possibly with functional consequences.
evidence: Inference from observations in C. elegans

claim: The dendrites of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons are intertwined in bundles, and this arrangement has been proposed to help synchronize hormone release.
source: For example, the dendrites of gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons are intertwined in bundles, and this arrangement has been proposed to help synchronize hormone release (Campbell et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2009

claim: Neuropeptide-releasing neurons in Drosophila that serve as circadian pacemakers undergo daily changes in axon fasciculation, driven by cycling expression levels of the NCAM adhesion molecule FAS2.
source: In a possibly related example, neuropeptide-releasing neurons in Drosophila that serve as circadian pacemakers undergo daily changes in axon fasciculation, driven by cycling expression levels of the NCAM adhesion molecule FAS2 (Fernández et al., 2008; Sivachenko et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fernández et al., 2008 and Sivachenko et al., 2013

claim: Genetically manipulating FAS2 expression to force constitutive defasciculation leads to changes in circadian behavior.
source: Interestingly, genetically manipulating FAS2 expression to force constitutive defasciculation leads to changes in circadian behavior, suggesting that fasciculation may indeed affect neuronal activity (Sivachenko et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sivachenko et al., 2013

claim: Ferenczi et al. used an engineering approach to optogenetically manipulate ion flow in hippocampal and cortical axons and observed a 'bystander' effect on the membrane current of neighboring axons, independent of synaptic transmission.
source: Consistent with this notion, Ferenczi et al. used an engineering approach to optogenetically manipulate ion flow in hippocampal and cortical axons and observed a 'bystander' effect on the membrane current of neighboring axons, independent of synaptic transmission (Ferenczi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferenczi et al., 2016

claim: In wild-type Drosophila, a short pulse of odor-induced activity in one olfactory dendrite inhibited tonic firing of its bundled neighbor, independently of chemical or electrical synapses.
source: Remarkably, in wild-type Drosophila, Carlson and colleagues demonstrated similar ephaptic effects between bundled olfactory dendrites (Su et al., 2012): a short pulse of odor-induced activity in one of these dendrites inhibited tonic firing of its bundled neighbor, independently of chemical or electrical synapses.
evidence: Supported by citation to Su et al., 2012

claim: Ephaptic effects between bundled olfactory dendrites in Drosophila can alter behavioral responses.
source: Importantly, they showed that this ephaptic effect could even alter behavioral responses.
evidence: Supported by reference to Su et al., 2012 study

claim: Amphid sensilla in other nematode species such as Acrobeles complexus, Strongyloides stercoralis, and Haemonchus contortus exhibit well-ordered bundles, albeit with configurations that are different from each other and from C. elegans.
source: Interestingly, amphid sensilla in other nematode species such as Acrobeles complexus, Strongyloides stercoralis, and Haemonchus contortus also exhibit well-ordered bundles, albeit with configurations that are different from each other and from C. elegans (Bumbarger et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bumbarger et al., 2009

claim: The diversity of amphid bundle structures in different nematode species may have arisen partly through altered expression of a small number of CAMs.
source: It is interesting to speculate whether this diversity of structures may have arisen partly through altered expression of a small number of CAMs.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the study's findings
